title: What is the difference between a monolith and microservices?
description: One deployable vs many small services — deployment, scaling, data, and team-topology trade-offs, plus why 'start monolith, split later' is the common advice.

data.text: **Question:** What is the difference between a monolith and microservices?

A **monolith** is one deployable application whose parts (UI, business logic, data access) run together in one process and share one database — changes are local calls, deployment is one unit. **Microservices** split the business capabilities into small, independently deployable services, each owning its data and communicating over the network. Microservices buy independent scaling, deployment, and team autonomy — and pay for it with network failure modes, distributed data complexity, and operational overhead. The architecture is a trade-off, not an upgrade.

**What actually differs:**
- **Deployment**: monolith = one artifact, atomic releases (and atomic rollbacks); services = dozens of independent release trains and version skew between callers
- **Data**: monolith shares one transactional DB (easy ACID across modules); services each own their data — cross-service work becomes sagas, events, and eventual consistency
- **Communication**: in-process calls vs network calls that can time out, be retried, and be duplicated — the network turns 'it returned an error' into 'did it happen or not?'
- **Scaling**: monolith scales the whole app; services scale the hot one (the image resizer) alone
- **Teams**: Conway's Law — services let each team own and deploy its slice without coordinating releases
- **Failure**: a monolith crash takes everything down; a service failure must be absorbed by timeouts, circuit breakers, and degraded features

**Costs people underestimate:** distributed tracing and alerting across services, contract/version management, deployment pipelines per service, and the 'nano-service' trap — splitting so fine that every feature touches six services and nothing ships without coordinated deploys.

**The pragmatic path:** most successful teams start with a well-structured monolith (modular boundaries enforced in code), extract services only where a real driver exists — independent scaling, different lifecycles, or team ownership. Strangler-fig lets you peel modules out incrementally.

data.title: Same feature, two architectures
Don't buy the architecture, buy the driver
data.text: 'We might scale one part differently someday' is not a driver — neither is résumé-driven development. Real drivers: a module that needs 10x the compute, teams blocking each other on releases, or a subsystem that must fail independently. Without a driver, a monolith with clean module boundaries gives you most of the benefit and none of the distributed-systems tax.

Interviewers want to hear:
- Not 'monolith = old, microservices = modern' — a balanced trade-off answer
- At least two costs: distributed data/transactions, network failure modes, operational overhead
- The independence benefits: deployment, scaling, team ownership
- Pragmatism: start monolith, extract with a real driver (strangler fig)

items: Presenting microservices as strictly better — ignoring consistency and ops costs
Calling any multi-project solution 'microservices' — deployment independence is the test
Splitting services by technical layer (a 'UI service', a 'database service') instead of by business capability
Underestimating what replaces ACID: sagas, outbox, idempotency, reconciliation
Forgetting observability — distributed systems without tracing are undebuggable
How do services share data without sharing a database?
What is a saga and when do you need one?
How does Conway's Law relate to service boundaries?
What is the strangler fig pattern?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Monolith: one deployable, one DB, local calls, atomic transactions
Microservices: independent deploys and scaling, at the price of network + distributed data
Cross-service ACID becomes sagas, events, and eventual consistency
Start monolith with clear module seams; extract services only with a real driver
data.takeaway: Microservices are an organizational and operational trade — the network is the tax you pay for independent deployment.
